question: In a child with PPRP, the tibialis anterior and peronei are paralysed but the gastrocnemius-soleus complex and tibialis posterior are intact. Which deformity is most likely to develop?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Calcaneus results when the gastrocnemius-soleus is paralysed while the dorsiflexors are intact. Here the gastrocnemius-soleus is intact, so it will pull the foot into equinus, not calcaneus.
Valgus results from loss of invertors (tibialis posterior) with intact evertors (peroneals). Here peroneals are also paralysed, so the foot will not deviate into valgus.

Correct. Paralysis of tibialis anterior (dorsiflexor) and peroneals (evertors), with intact gastrocnemius-soleus (plantarflexion) and tibialis posterior (inversion), produces the classic equinovarus: the foot is held plantarflexed and inverted.

A flail foot requires paralysis of ALL muscle groups around the ankle. Here gastrocnemius-soleus and tibialis posterior are intact; their unopposed action will produce a predictable equinovarus deformity.

overallFeedback.feedback: Map the forces: intact gastrocnemius-soleus = plantarflexion force (equinus); intact tibialis posterior = inversion force (varus); paralysed tibialis anterior and peroneals = no opposing dorsiflexion or eversion. The resultant is equinovarus.

Excellent analysis. Muscle charting predicts deformity: the intact muscle groups (gastrocnemius-soleus plantarflexes; tibialis posterior inverts) are unopposed, producing equinovarus — the most common foot deformity in PPRP.
